title: Lesson 18: Spotting the Automatable Tasks in Your Own Job
description: An audit for finding the slices of your own week that are worth handing to a tool: task definitions, the four signals of an automatable task, and a payback calculation you can run on any candidate.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Spotting the Automatable Tasks in Your Own Job", which question actually pays off?
options: Not whether your job is automatable, but which of the tasks in your job are automatable
Whether your whole occupation can be fully automated
Which of your colleagues' jobs are automatable
Whether the tool is cheaper than hiring someone
questions.explanation: The lesson says asking whether your job is automatable is too big to be useful, because a job is a bundle of dozens of small recurring tasks and only some of them are automatable.

questions.question: What research finding does the lesson cite about automation potential?
options: Most occupations can already be fully automated
Fewer than 5 percent of occupations could be fully automated with then-current technology, while about half of the activities people are paid to do had the technical potential to be automated
Automation potential is highest in the tasks that need the most judgment
Roughly 80 percent of occupations are fully automatable
questions.explanation: The lesson cites the McKinsey Global Institute work on activities rather than occupations, and uses it to argue that almost every job is a mix, so the real question is which slices are automatable.

questions.question: The lesson gives four signals of an automatable task. Which one belongs on that list?
options: The task is performed by more than one person
The task is highly visible to leadership
You can write the steps down and someone else, or a tool, could follow them without asking you a single question
The task takes at least a full working day
questions.explanation: That is the signal about writing the steps down, which the lesson pairs with frequency, and with the judgment call as its opposite: a decision that depends on context, values, or relationships you own is not a rule.
